Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Stress: Stress, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Dr. Nguyen, a 77-year-old retired surgeon of South Eastern Asian descent, sat in his armchair, his eyes fixed on some distant point as he recounted the day that changed him forever. It was during a hospital shift when a massive fire broke out in the operating room next door, claiming the lives of several patients and staff members. Dr. Nguyen had been mere feet away, powerless to stop the inferno from spreading. The memory of that day still felt like an out-of-body experience; he couldn't shake off the feeling that it had happened to someone else. As he spoke, his wife of 50 years, Mrs. Nguyen, listened attentively in the adjacent room, her expression a mix of concern and sadness. She had grown accustomed to her husband's sudden mood swings, but she knew that something was amiss when he started avoiding their favorite TV shows and movies. He couldn't bear watching anything related to fires or hospitals, fearing it would transport him back to that fateful day. The smallest details could trigger Dr. Nguyen's memories: the sensation of heat on his skin, which always made him feel like he was reliving that moment; the acrid smell of burnt flesh and smoke, which lingered in his nostrils long after the fire had been extinguished. Even stress itself became a potent trigger, leaving him feeling jumpy and on edge. In an effort to cope, Dr. Nguyen pushed away any positive emotions that arose, deeming them "unsafe" and "untrustworthy." He couldn't allow himself to feel happy or content, fearing it would make him vulnerable to another traumatic event. His mind became a battlefield, constantly fighting to suppress thoughts of the fire. When his grandchildren visited, he struggled to engage in playful activities, worried that laughter and joy would somehow undo the defenses he had built around himself. As time passed, Dr. Nguyen began taking more risks than usual – driving recklessly, ignoring safety protocols at home – as if tempting fate or trying to prove a point. He knew it was irrational, but his body seemed to be reacting of its own accord, perpetually on high alert for potential dangers. Sudden noises made him flinch; the sound of sirens in the distance sent his heart racing. At times, Dr. Nguyen felt like he was living with an alien entity inside his head – a constant presence that stirred up memories without warning. He couldn't quite put those memories in order, and when they did surface, they were fragmented and disjointed. The emotions accompanying these flashbacks were overwhelming, leaving him gasping for breath. Dr. Nguyen's inner world had become a minefield of self-doubt and fear. He saw his own body as an enemy, always reacting to threats that weren't there. He questioned his competence as a person, wondering if he was somehow defective or flawed. The constant vigilance he maintained left him exhausted, but he couldn't shake off the feeling that disaster lurked around every corner. It wasn't until Dr. Nguyen's wife convinced him to see a therapist that he began to confront the depths of his trauma. As he sat in the therapist's office, he knew it was time to face the memories and emotions he had been avoiding for so long. With a mix of trepidation and hope, he embarked on this new journey, unsure what lay ahead but determined to reclaim control over his life. Dr. Nguyen's eyes finally met those of the therapist as he whispered, "I'm tired of living like this. I want to learn how to live again." The words hung in the air like a challenge, and for the first time in years, Dr. Nguyen felt a glimmer of hope that he might one day find peace.
